item.title: On the NP-Hardness of Rank-Metric Minimum Distance and Syndrome Decoding, at Every Rate
item.description: arXiv:2610.40825v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this work, we investigate the hardness of computing minimum distance, as well as the hardness of syndrome decoding, for rank-metric codes. It is known (Gaborit and Z\'emor, IEEE TIT 2016) that for $\mathbb{F}_{q^m}$-linear rank-metric codes of length $N$, minimum distance when $m=O(N)$ and syndrome decoding when $m=O(N^2)$ are NP-hard under randomized reductions. We obtain a derandomization of these results and a bit more. We show that for any fixed small $\varepsilon>0$, for $\mathbb{F}_{q^m}$-linear rank-metric codes of length $N$ with $m=O(N^{1+\varepsilon})$, the problems of minimum distance, nearest codeword, and syndrome decoding are NP-hard under deterministic reductions. Further, we can prescribe the rate; that is, if we restrict to codes having any fixed rational rate $R\in(0,1)$, then the NP-hardness for all three problems persists. Our main technical contribution is simple, and possibly of independent interest. The reduction of Gaborit and Z\'emor (IEEE TIT 2016) relies on a distance-preserving embedding of a Hamming-metric code into a rank-metric code, obtained by multiplying its coordinates by a uniformly random vector. We show that we can choose an explicit vector from a slightly larger extension field.
item.dc:creator: Venkata Gandikota, Vatsal Jha, S. Venkitesh

item.title: Lowered crossover points of Anthropic's subexponential 3-SAT algorithm
item.description: arXiv:2610.41622v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The October 2026 refutations of the Exponential Time Hypothesis count satisfying assignments in time $2^{o(n)}$, but an asymptotic bound does not say from which input size, the crossover point, they beat the best known algorithms. We make the #3-SAT recursion of Anthropic's algorithm explicit and lower its crossover points, computed from the main term of the proved bound, by proved changes. For the bound in the number $m$ of clauses, at clause density one, the crossover point drops to about $2^{420}$ clauses from $2^{33858}$; for general 3-SAT, in the number $n$ of variables, our estimate drops to $2^{8.6\cdot10^9}$ variables from $2^{2.2\cdot10^{12}}$. With integer tables the recursion counts, for every $j$, the assignments satisfying exactly $j$ clauses in time $2^{O(m/\sqrt{\log m})}$. We observe that this refutes the Sparse Max-3-SAT Hypothesis of Alman and Vassilevska Williams, which also follows from either refutation by the reduction of Impagliazzo, Paturi and Zane, and we lower the crossover point of this computation to about $2^{1016}$ clauses from $2^{68364}$. The distance is structural: we define a rewrite-and-merge class that contains the recursion and all our constructions, and prove that in the main-term model no grid algorithm in it can gain for general 3-SAT below about $2^{6000}$ variables. For two balanced homogeneous merges we prove with quantum functionals an exponent of at least $(\log_2K)^{-3}$ per edge bit, which excludes running times $2^{n^{1-c}}$. Independently of SAT, we formalise the algorithm as a model of computation, Signed Network Sums, which contains rank-one methods and contraction trees. On the complete graph with four nodes, one-level constructions contract the network in $N^{23/6}$ if $\omega=2$ and in about $N^{3.93}$ on the current (preprint) matrix-multiplication curve, below the bound $N^4$ of every rank-one method or contraction tree.
item.dc:creator: Ruhollah Majdoddin

item.title: Catalytic space-efficient algorithms for Distance and Determinant
item.description: arXiv:2610.41723v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Catalytic computation reuses potentially large but in-use space (or catalytic space) which must be restored to its initial contents while the clean space is small. This allows all problems in $\mathsf{NL}$ and even larger classes to be in catalytic logspace [Buhrman et al, STOC2014]. In [Chmel et al, CCC2026] the catalytic space for reachability was restricted to sublinear space (specifically, $n \big/ 2^{\theta(\sqrt{\log n})}$ space) while remaining in polynomial time. This matches the non-catalytic bounds from [Barnes et al, SICOMP1998]. We extend the reachability bound to shortest distance, proving a simultaneous sublinear catalytic space and polynomial time bound (henceforth called, sublinear $\mathsf{CLP}$). This is the first simultaneous sublinear space and polynomial time bound for distance even without the catalytic discipline. Moreover, our bound works even for polynomially weighted graphs. Along the way we prove simultaneous near linear catalytic space ($\mathcal{O}(n\log^{O(1)}{n})$) and polynomial time bounds for the determinant. We also show some applications to planar matching problems. Our starting point was catalytic computation of reachability in directed graphs by [Cook-Pyne, ITCS2026]. [Edenhofer, arXiv:2602.21088] used it to give a tradeoff between catalytic and non-catalytic space, while [Chmel et al, CCC2026] compress the graph to a smaller graph preserving $s,t$-reachability to achieve a smaller space bound. All three can be modified to yield an algorithm for unweighted distance. Our contribution is to define an approximation to the walk polynomial in weighted graphs that allows us to infer weighted $s,t$-distance in sublinear $\mathsf{CLP}$. We do so by non-trivially combining elements from each of the above three papers.
item.dc:creator: Srijan Chakraborty, Samir Datta, Kushagra Shandilya

item.title: Counting Square Tilings with a Fixed Set of Polyominoes Is #EXP-Complete
item.description: arXiv:2610.42063v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The gap between feasibility and exact counting raises a fundamental question about how much information an input must carry to sustain computational hardness. We show that this separation persists even when the geometric rules are fixed and each instance is specified solely by the binary side length of a square. Specifically, there exists a fixed finite family of connected polyominoes whose translation-only square-tiling counting function is #EXP-complete under polynomial-time metric reductions and belongs to #E. Since tileability for any fixed polyomino family is decidable in polynomial time, this result establishes a striking separation between feasibility and exact counting under highly restricted geometric inputs. The proof develops a two-stage numerical isolation technique that recovers accepting-computation counts from a boundary-amplified Wang system and preserves them through a rigid geometric compiler that controls all noncanonical polyomino tilings.
item.dc:creator: Qiuyu Chen, Baao Xie

item.title: Approximate Polynomial Satisfiability and Integral Closure Membership in the Counting Hierarchy
item.description: arXiv:2610.42138v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Andrews, Garg, and Schost recently, in a breakthrough result, placed Hilbert's Nullstellensatz (HN) in the Counting Hierarchy ($\CH$) using constant-depth circuits for multivariate resultants. While HN deals with exact polynomial satisfiability, Guo, Saxena, and Sinhababu (CCC~2018; Theory of Computing~2019) introduced approximate polynomial satisfiability (APS) as a natural approximative analogue of polynomial system satisfiability. They proved its $\mathsf{NP}$-hardness and a $\PSPACE$ upper bound, and used APS to construct hitting sets for $\overline{\mathsf{VP}}$ in polynomial space, substantially narrowing the GCT chasm in geometric complexity theory. We place APS in the Counting Hierarchy for rational polynomials given by arithmetic circuits. Our proof combines Noether normalization with a geometric restriction on how points in the image of a polynomial map approach the origin, reducing APS to a test on multivariate resultants which allows solvability in $\CH$. It complements the independent and concurrent proofs of Balaji, Shirmohammadi, Tavenas, and Worrell, and Andrews, Garg, Oliveira, and Schost. Moreover, we also place integral closure membership testing in the Counting Hierarchy. Here, the question is whether a given polynomial $f$ is integral over $\C[f_1,\ldots,f_m]$. Our approach uses a global annihilator criterion and an effective degree bound to reduce non-integrality to APS in polynomial time.
item.dc:creator: Sanyam Agarwal, Archit Hari, Anurag Pandey, Himanshu Shukla

item.title: Adversarial Wronskians: A proof of the Kung--Traub conjecture
item.description: arXiv:2610.40660v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We prove the Kung--Traub conjecture: a deterministic stationary root-finding method without memory, using at most $n$ real scalar function or derivative evaluations per iteration, cannot have local order greater than $2^{n-1}$ on every real analytic function with a simple zero. For $n\geq2$, the bound is attained by the methods of Kung and Traub. The local estimate is required at every sufficiently close starting point, with constants that may depend on the function. Evaluation points and derivative orders may be chosen adaptively, and the rules for choosing them and processing the data are unrestricted. The proof uses a localisation property of polynomial Wronskians to obtain a lower bound at each fixed scale. A diagonal construction then gives one entire function, with derivative bounded above and below on the real line, for which every larger order fails. We also obtain a sharper bound when evaluations are made in prescribed groups, and prove the corresponding result for complex scalar evaluations. The results of this paper are also formally verified in Lean.
item.dc:creator: Matthew J. Colbrook

item.title: Clifford synthesis is NP-complete
item.description: arXiv:2610.40886v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We show that the problem of synthesizing a quantum circuit for a given Clifford operator using at most a specified amount of resources is NP-complete for several resource models of practical interest. Specifically, we study synthesis of a given Clifford operator using single-qubit Clifford gates and two-qubit Clifford gates, with full qubit connectivity and no additional ancilla qubits. With single-qubit gates free and CNOT as the only two-qubit gate, we show that deciding whether a given target admits an implementation using at most a specified number of CNOT gates is NP-complete, and we show that the problem remains NP-complete when any two-qubit Clifford gate is allowed and the budget counts all such gates. Moreover, we show that both results continue to hold when SWAP gates may be inserted for free, and when single-qubit gates are also considered part of the budget. In each case, we build on recent work by Li and Guan and show that there are polynomial-time reductions from Hamiltonian path in grid graphs to these decision problems, using a number of qubits quadratic in the number of grid vertices.
item.dc:creator: S{\o}ren Fuglede J{\o}rgensen

item.title: Faster #PPM from faster #3SAT
item.description: arXiv:2610.41048v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The counting variant (#PPM) of the permutation pattern matching (PPM) problem asks for the number of occurrences of a permutation pattern in a host permutation of length $n$. The problem admits faster algorithms than the trivial $O^*(2^n)$ time enumeration; the best known running time, for both PPM and #PPM, is $O(1.415^n)$ (Gawrychowski and Rzepecki). It is also known that PPM is ETH-hard: an algorithm with running time $2^{o(n/\log{n})}$ would imply a subexponential algorithm for 3SAT (Jel\'{i}nek, Opler, and Pek\'{a}rek). We give a reduction in the opposite direction, showing that an algorithm for counting satisfying assignments of a 3-CNF formula (#3SAT) in time $2^{O({n}/{f(n)})}$, where $n$ is the number of variables, yields an algorithm for #PPM with running time $2^{O({n \sqrt{\log{f(n)}/{f(n)}}})}$. In particular, the recently claimed refutation of ETH by OpenAI implies a #3SAT algorithm with an improvement factor $f(n) \in \Omega(\sqrt{\log{n}}/\log\log{n})$ in the exponent; this yields, through our reduction, a subexponential algorithm for #PPM.
item.dc:creator: L\'aszl\'o Kozma

item.title: Stochastic and Noisy Oracles in Smooth Continuous Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2610.41086v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We review models of inexact computational oracles in smooth continuous optimization and their implications for the convergence, computational complexity, and attainable accuracy of optimization algorithms. We adopt a framework in which zeroth-,first-, and second-order oracles are characterized by quantitative error bounds and may accept additional control parameters that influence both their accuracy and computational cost. We introduce deterministic and stochastic oracle models and illustrate their properties through a variety of examples, including finite-difference approximations, stochastic gradients, and randomized derivative estimators. Particular attention is given to the distinction between absolute and relative errors, bias and variance, and stochastic function evaluations with independent or coupled randomness. A central theme of the review is the use of common analytical tools to recover and compare convergence and complexity guarantees under different oracle models. For deterministic and stochastic first-order methods, we show how a general descent inequality leads to complexity bounds under various assumptions on the objective function and all proposed oracle models. In the stochastic setting, we develop bounds on expected stopping times and the accuracy that can be guaranteed under different oracle conditions. We also examine the total computational complexity of algorithms relying on specific oracle constructions and briefly review models of inexact second- order information and their use in optimization algorithms.
item.dc:creator: Albert S. Berahas, Liyuan Cao, Katya Scheinberg

item.title: Exponential quantum-classical query separations for cyclic Forrelation
item.description: arXiv:2610.41694v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the randomized classical query complexity of cyclic Forrelation, a cyclic analogue of $k$-Forrelation [AA15, STOC'15; BS21, STOC'21]. Given $k$ Boolean functions $f_1,\ldots,f_k:\mathbb{F}_2^n\to\{-1,1\}$, the goal is to estimate $T_k=N^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}(D_{f_1}H^{\otimes n}\cdots D_{f_k}H^{\otimes n}),$ where $D_{f_i}=\operatorname{diag}(f_i(x):x\in\mathbb{F}_2^n)$, $H$ is the Hadamard gate, and $N=2^n$. This normalized-trace problem can be solved with $k$ quantum queries in the DQC1 model. Its classical query complexity was left open in [JLS+26, FOCS'26], which conjectured a lower bound of $\widetilde{\Omega}(N^{1-2/k})$. We establish a nearly complete characterization of the nonadaptive classical query complexity of cyclic Forrelation. For even $k\ge 4$, we prove a tight bound of $\Theta_k(N^{1-2/k})$ for constant additive error. For odd $k\ge 5$, we obtain a lower bound of $\Omega_k(N^{1-2/(k-1)})$ and an upper bound of $O_k(N^{1-2/k})$. Surprisingly, $k=3$ admits a polylogarithmic-query nonadaptive classical algorithm, disproving the conjecture in this case. These results suggest an unexpected parity-dependent structure: the nonadaptive complexity may be governed by the independence number of the $k$-cycle, leading to the exponent $1-1/\lfloor k/2\rfloor$, rather than the previously conjectured $1-2/k$, which was motivated by a Fourier-growth heuristic. Finally, allowing adaptivity, we prove a lower bound of $\Omega(N^{1/4})$ for every $k\ge4$. Although formally close to $k$-Forrelation, the cyclic structure leads to rather different classical behavior and requires different techniques. Our lower bounds are based on hidden-shift collision constructions, and our upper bounds follow from randomized sampling together with cycle-specific conditional-moment estimates. Our results provide a systematic understanding of its query advantages over classical computation.
item.dc:creator: Yuxin Zhang, Changpeng Shao

item.title: Treedepth is NP-Hard on Planar Graphs of Maximum Degree 3
item.description: arXiv:2610.42033v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Treedepth is an important parameter in algorithmic graph theory. It is known that the problem of computing the treedepth of a graph is NP-hard. It has been an open problem whether treedepth can be computed in polynomial time when the input graph is restricted to be planar, or of bounded degree. Assuming $P \neq NP$, we answer both questions in the negative: Under polynomial-time Turing reductions, it is NP-hard to compute the treedepth of planar graphs with maximum degree 3. This degree bound is best possible, since treedepth can be computed efficiently on graphs of maximum degree 2.
item.dc:creator: Kolja K\"uhn

item.title: A Relative-Computability Theory of Self-Improving Agents
item.description: arXiv:2605.27381v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Self-improving agents can acquire a procedure without knowing when its supporting teacher can safely be removed. We extend an oracle-relative model of evolving agents with explicit acquisition and completion contracts, separating learning a solver from certifying its independence. For a known finite-dimensional Boolean feature language, a query history determines exactly the answers in its feature span. A guarded protocol permits query-proposer revision while guaranteeing completion with the optimal number of teacher calls, and a supplied separating specification gives a finite-family extension. The resulting solver answers every input without its teacher and remains in the baseline computability layer. The central obstruction concerns supplying the completion specification: no baseline-effective procedure can extract a valid span or separating specification uniformly from arbitrary total programs, already in one feature dimension or with two candidate descriptions. Classical relative computation and limiting-revision results locate these claims without imposing a ceiling on practical improvement. Controlled experiments distinguish exact teacher removal from low-risk stopping and measure adaptation benefits and costs against a stronger greedy baseline. The framework makes the information required to acquire, certify, and deploy a capability explicit.
item.dc:creator: Chien-Ping Lu

item.title: Matrix Multiplication from Polynomial Packings: A Constructive and Elementary Proof of $\omega\le9/4$
item.description: arXiv:2610.28627v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We give a self-contained constructive proof that the matrix multiplication exponent satisfies $\omega\le9/4$. In a recent breakthrough, OpenAI~\cite{original} established this bound in the model of exact scalar arithmetic over the complex numbers, using non-constructive arguments in Strassen's asymptotic spectral framework. We explicitly construct a Strassen-style matrix multiplication identity and obtain the bound by ordinary block recursion. For every $\gamma>0$, the resulting algorithm multiplies two $n\times n$ integer matrices using $O(n^{9/4+\gamma})$ integer arithmetic operations. As an independent contribution, we develop a framework of \emph{polynomial packings}---methods for reducing many polynomial multiplications to fewer ones using linear operations. We isolate and generalize a construction of OpenAI~\cite{original} to obtain a simple packing, and show how packings can be composed to amplify their ``compression rate", which finally yields Strassen-like identities.
item.dc:creator: Rafael Pass

item.title: Turnstile Streaming Algorithms Might (Still) as Well Be Linear Sketches, for Polynomial-Length Streams
item.description: arXiv:2604.22052v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A fundamental question in streaming complexity is whether every space-efficient turnstile algorithm is implicitly a linear sketch. The work of Li, Nguyen, and Woodruff (STOC~2014) established an equivalence between the two, but their reduction requires a stream length that is at least doubly exponential in the dimension $n$. In the opposite direction, Kallaugher and Price (STOC~2020) showed a separation for streams of linear length, so the equivalence does not hold in general. The most natural and practically relevant regime, that of polynomial-length streams, has therefore remained open. We show that polynomial-length turnstile algorithms admit linear-sketch simulations. More precisely, if a turnstile algorithm uses $S$ bits of space and succeeds on all streams of length $\textrm{poly}(D, n)$, then on final vectors $x$ with $\|x\|_2 \le D$, its output can be recovered from $O(S)$ linear measurements of $x$, using $O(S)$ bits overall. For smooth problems under appropriate input distributions, a mollified version of the reduction yields a bounded-entry sketch with $O(S / \log D)$ measurements and optimal $O(S)$ total space. Our results extend to strict turnstile streams and non-uniform Read-Once Branching Programs (ROBPs). Instead of the transition-graph arguments of prior work, our proof uses Fourier analysis and tools from additive combinatorics to extract discrete linear measurements. We show that an $S$-bit algorithm can only be sensitive to a small set of heavy Fourier frequencies, which lie close to a finite group of order $2^{O(S)}$, and we use generators of this group as the rows of the sketching matrix. Combined with existing lower bounds for real sketches and for communication, this gives new lower bounds for polynomial-length turnstile streams.
item.dc:creator: Cheng Jiang, Yinchen Liu, Huacheng Yu

item.title: No Size-Preserving Amplification with Quantum Advice
item.description: arXiv:2610.03377v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Marriott and Watrous showed that quantum Merlin--Arthur games admit generic error reduction without increasing witness size [Computational Complexity, 2005]. In this work, we show that this state-size-preserving amplification property does not hold for polynomial-time quantum computation with quantum advice. In particular, we present decision problems for which even a vanishing additive error reduction requires longer advice. More precisely, for every polynomially bounded advice length $m(n)=\omega(1)$ and every error bound $\varepsilon(n)$ that stays below $1/2$ by at least an inverse polynomial, there is a positive function $\delta$ with $\delta(n)=O\bigl(\min\{(\log m/m)^{1/4},\ \sqrt{\log m/m}\,/(1/2-\varepsilon(n))\}\bigr)$ such that $\mathsf{BQP}_{\varepsilon}/\mathsf{q}m \subsetneq \mathsf{BQP}_{\varepsilon + \delta}/\mathsf{q}m$; for constant $\varepsilon$ the gap is $O(\sqrt{\log m/m})$. Here, $\mathsf{BQP}_\varepsilon/\mathsf{q}m$ is the class of languages recognizable with error at most $\varepsilon(n)$ by a polynomial-time quantum algorithm with an $m(n)$-qubit advice state that only depends on the input length $n$. We show this by proving a stronger separation $\mathsf{P}_{\varepsilon+\delta}/\mathsf{r} m \not\subset \mathsf{BQP}_{\varepsilon}/\mathsf{q} m$, where $\mathsf{P}_{\varepsilon}/\mathsf{r}m$ is the class of languages recognizable with error at most $\varepsilon(n)$ by a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm with an $m(n)$-bit advice string sampled from a distribution that depends only on $n$.
item.dc:creator: Shih-Han Hung, Han-Hsuan Lin

item.title: Verification and Self-Improvement in Agentic AI: Foundations and Limits
item.description: arXiv:2610.10611v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A self-improving agent can find accepted solutions more often without expanding the tasks its verification interface can accept. We extend task-relative verification with explicit support and transcript interfaces to distinguish search gains from changes in accepted-task coverage. A stage's native reach contains tasks accepted with default support; its closure frontier contains tasks accepted with any support the declared interface permits. A semantic containment criterion identifies the authority or exposure condition that every verified escape must violate, while guard-transfer invariance prevents a change of representation from being counted as a capability expansion. An executable Boolean-program repair agent makes the distinction concrete: over 36,864 paired runs, counterexample feedback reduces verifier calls without changing coverage, whereas an enforced permission change admits a new target with a proof excluding every old-interface program. Exact and uniformly gapped randomized verification share this account; independent majority amplification improves reliability while preserving the accepted language. Separate adaptive-selection contracts state what is additionally required to interpret a proposed successor's score as evidence of deployment improvement. Classical hierarchy results and finite audits provide supporting boundaries. The framework specifies the evidence needed to establish improved search, wider accepted capability, and reliable successor selection.
item.dc:creator: Chien-Ping Lu

item.title: Simple Strategy-Iteration with Dantzig's Rule is not Strongly Polynomial on Turn-Based Deterministic Games
item.description: arXiv:2610.27386v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study turn-based deterministic zero-sum games with discounted and long-run average costs. For discounted costs, we establish exponential and superpolynomial iteration lower bounds for the simple strategy-iteration method with Dantzig's rule under unrestricted costs and unit weights, respectively. To the best of our knowledge, we establish for the first time that the method is not strongly polynomial, and this remains true even when all action costs belong to $\{-1,0,1\}$. For long-run average costs, we extend the Dantzig counterpart in~\cite{zhongye2026} to the two-player setting and prove that it terminates at an optimal strategy profile. However, a similar counterexample construction establishes an exponential iteration lower bound for termination with unrestricted costs. This construction does not extend to unit weights, for which we prove that the algorithm admits a strongly polynomial implementation.
item.dc:creator: Sanyou Mei

item.title: Maxwell's equations are universal for sparse linear algebra
item.description: arXiv:2610.38913v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Optical and wave-based analog computing has re-emerged as a route to accelerating linear algebra, with metamaterials and photonic circuits shown to invert matrices and solve integral equations. However, it has remained unclear which problems such passive structures can represent, and at what cost, once encoding, precision, conditioning and readout are accounted for. Here, we show that every polynomially conditioned sparse linear system can be compiled into a three-dimensional dielectric -- a cavity filled with lossless, isotropic material of bounded permittivity -- whose time-harmonic response encodes its solution. For $m$ nonzero coefficients, the volume of the structure and the cost of writing it down and reading out the answer scale as $\tilde O(m^{3/2})$, coefficients require only $O(\log m)$ bits, and every field that approximately satisfies Maxwell's equations decodes to an approximate solution. We prove the construction for the continuum equations and give a computer-assisted version for the Yee discretization underlying finite-difference solvers. Read in reverse, it implies that electromagnetic simulation is, up to this overhead, as hard as general sparse linear algebra: a sufficiently fast general-purpose Maxwell solver would yield a faster sparse linear solver.
item.dc:creator: Yannick Augenstein
